column3: A Japanese soroban (abacus): the time is the bead pattern on the rods. The upper "heaven" bead and lower "earth" beads on each rod SET that digit; each minute the beads flick across and click into the new number, the whole rack riffles through on the hour.

A slide rule: the inner scale slides past the fixed scale and a glass cursor with a hairline crosses a set of division marks; the reading under the hairline is the time. Each minute the slide eases to a new setting with a soft click of the cursor.

An orb-weaver's web strung across a window frame at dawn, beaded with dew: the radial threads and the spiral ARE the numerals, anchored between frames. Each minute the spider cuts the changed thread and walks the new one out; a draught makes the whole web shiver.

A dandelion clock: the seed head's pappi make up the time, and a breath of wind lifts the seeds off and carries them into the new formation. On the hour the whole head blows away and a fresh one opens.
A bank vault door: the spoked dial spins, the tumblers fall, the bolts retract and the door swings open on the new minute. On the hour the door slams and the dial spins a full combination.

A pinball machine: a steel ball ricochets off bumpers and drops the lit targets that spell the time. On the minute the ball knocks the old digits down and the flippers knock the new ones up; the hour is a multiball.
An ancient water clock (clepsydra): water drips from a jar into a marked vessel and the floating surface carries the time; the minute turn is a drip that ripples the water into the new number.

A cuckoo clock: a carved wooden chalet, leaf chains and pinecone weights, hand-carved numerals, and the bird that pops from its doors. On the hour the doors fly open and the cuckoo calls; each minute the weights drag a hairline down the chains.

A letterpress: a compositor's stick of loose lead type, inked, locked in the chase and pressed onto paper; the printed sheet is the time, mirror-image in the type. Each minute the type is redistributed, reset, and a fresh impression pulled.
A turntable: vinyl spins and the groove is a spiral the stylus rides; the pressed ridges in the groove carry the numerals. On the minute the stylus jumps a track with a crackle.
A constellation chart of the night sky: stars are joined by sight-lines into the time, the sky drifts slowly round the pole star, and a shooting star crosses out a changed digit.
The aurora borealis over a black ridge: curtains of light ripple and fold, and the time is where the green light thickens. On the minute a substorm surges and the curtains re-hang as the new number.

A Go board (goban): black and white stones on the 19x19 grid spell the time (rings for white, solid discs for black). A hand plays a stone a second; the minute turn captures the old number off the board.
A telegraph office: a brass key taps and a sounder clacks the time in Morse dots and dashes, and the paper tape carries the numerals as punched holes.
A beehive: comb cells fill with honey in the shape of the time, foragers land, and the waggle dance angles with the sun. On the minute the changed cell is capped with wax.

A zen gravel garden: a rake draws straight and concentric furrows in white gravel around set stones, and the time is the furrow pattern. Each minute the rake lifts and re-draws; the hour flood-rakes the garden fresh.
A fireworks display over a harbour: a shell climbs, bursts, and its stars hang as the time before drifting out. Each minute a new shell is fired; the hour is the finale.
A Ferris wheel at a night fair: the rim's cabins are lit windows, the wheel creeps round and the cabins read as the time; a full revolution on the hour.
A steam locomotive: the driving wheels, connecting rods and pistons work the time, the chuff from the stack marks the seconds, and the mileposts spell the hour.
A potter's wheel: clay is thrown and drawn up into the time's profile in cross-section; the wheel spins and the potter's hands shape the change on the minute.
